passage: Monday: at bath time Kashish, two, screamed “No!” and threw her towel. Avni snapped back “Stop shouting!” and the screams grew louder for ten minutes. Tuesday: Kashish yelled “No bath!” and Avni took a breath. “You're cross. Blue towel or green towel?” Kashish paused, still frowning. “Green.” Wednesday: she shouted “No!” once at the tap, then pointed to the yellow duck and said “Duck bath.” Avni laughed. “Duck bath, then.”

qa.q: What choice did Avni give Kashish on Tuesday?
qa.a: A blue towel or a green towel.

qa.q: What did Kashish's loud no seem to show she felt?
qa.a: It showed that she wanted control and was frustrated, not that she was defying Avni. She may also have been tired at bath time.

qa.q: What made Tuesday and Wednesday go better than Monday?
qa.a: Avni stayed calm, set the limit and gave a choice instead of shouting back, so Kashish had some power.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt on Monday and on Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday Avni probably felt frustrated and out of patience, and on Wednesday relieved and pleased that a small choice worked. 🙂

grounding: A toddler yells no when feeling powerless, and calm limits with choices reduce outbursts better than shouting back.

passage: Jasleen, two, reached for her mother's phone on the dining table and Alka lifted it out of reach. “No! NO!” Jasleen screamed, stamping, her face red. Alka knelt to her level. “You want the phone. It's not for playing. You can hold the spoon or the little book.” Jasleen wailed “No!” again, but more softly. Alka waited. Jasleen took the book, hiccuped and climbed on the chair. “Mine,” she said. “Yours,” Alka agreed.

qa.q: What did Alka offer Jasleen instead of the phone?
qa.a: The spoon or the little book.

qa.q: What do Jasleen's screams and stamping tell you about her feelings?
qa.a: They show frustration at being denied and a wish to have her own way. She may also be tired or hungry, which makes big feelings bigger.

qa.q: What could Alka do next time to reduce the outburst?
qa.a: She could put the phone away early and offer choices from the start.

qa.q: How might Jasleen see Alka's calm response?
qa.a: She may feel that her feelings are heard even though the limit stays. 🙂

grounding: A toddler screams no when denied and powerless, and the mother uses calm limits and choices rather than shouting back.

passage:
"Time to go home, Pema."
"NO! NO! NO!" Pema screamed from the top of the slide.
"Don't shout at your mother!" her father shouted.
"Shouting back won't help," said Sharmila quietly. She walked to the slide. "We're going home. Do you want to walk, or ride on my shoulders?"
Pema sniffed. "Shoulder."
"Shoulders it is."

qa.q: What choice did Sharmila offer Pema?
qa.a: To walk, or ride on her shoulders.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she screamed "NO!"?
qa.a: She was angry and upset about leaving the park and felt powerless to stop it.

qa.q: What worked better than shouting, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila's calm limit with a small choice worked, because Pema still had to go but felt some control, so she calmed down.

qa.q: How might Pema's father feel after seeing Sharmila's approach?
qa.a: He might feel a little embarrassed about shouting back, and see that calm worked better.

grounding: A toddler screams no at leaving the park, and her mother's calm limit with a choice works better than shouting back.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. When I said it was time to wash hands for lunch, Elizabeth yelled, "No! No!" and threw herself flat on the mat. I did not raise my voice. I crouched and held up two bars of soap. "Blue soap or green soap?" She stopped yelling and stared at them. Then she pointed at the green and walked to the sink with me. Choices seem to help her more than being told. Francis, daycare teacher

qa.q: Which soap did Elizabeth choose?
qa.a: The green soap.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when she threw herself flat and yelled?
qa.a: She was frustrated at being told to stop playing and felt she had no say; the choice seemed to make her calmer.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth's parents try at home, based on this note?
qa.a: Keep a calm voice and offer two small choices, like which soap or which cup, when a "no" outburst starts.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's parents feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and hopeful to learn a simple way to reduce her outbursts.

grounding: A teacher answers a toddler's loud "no" with a calm voice and a choice, which reduces the outburst.

passage:
Naveen sat on the tractor seat in the village yard, gripping the wheel. When Urmila, his grandmother, lifted him off, he screamed, "No! Mine! No!" and kicked his legs.
Urmila didn't shout back. She held him steady. "You love the tractor. It's going to the field now. Do you want to wave bye or honk the horn once?"
Naveen stopped mid-kick. "Honk." She held him up, he pressed it, and he waved as it rumbled off.

qa.q: What did Naveen choose to do?
qa.a: He chose to honk the horn once.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he screamed and kicked?
qa.a: He was angry and upset at being lifted off the tractor he loved, and felt powerless to stay.

qa.q: Which choice of Urmila's worked, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm and offering him a choice of how to say goodbye worked, because he got a little control and stopped screaming.

qa.q: What would change if Urmila had shouted at him to stop?
qa.a: Naveen would likely have screamed louder, and the goodbye would have ended in tears.

grounding: A grandmother answers a toddler's loud "no" with calm and a choice, which settles the outburst.

passage:
At the supermarket checkout in Cape Town, Lindiwe spotted the sweets. Zeynep said, “Not today.”
“NO! NO!” Lindiwe screamed, arching in the trolley seat.
A man behind them muttered, “Just shout louder than her.”
Zeynep didn't. She bent close and spoke low. “You really want sweets. The answer is no. Do you want to hold the bananas or the bread?”
Lindiwe's scream broke into hiccups. She looked at both, then grabbed the bananas.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe choose to hold?
qa.a: Lindiwe grabbed the bananas.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when she screamed "NO!"?
qa.a: She was angry and felt powerless at being refused the sweets, and screaming was the biggest way to say so without many words.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, the man's or Zeynep's, and why?
qa.a: Zeynep's calm, low voice, clear limit and small choice worked, because it gave Lindiwe some control without giving in; shouting back would likely have made it louder.

qa.q: How did the man behind them see the outburst?
qa.a: He saw it as a contest to win by shouting louder than her.

grounding: It illustrates a toddler screaming no when denied something and a parent using a calm limit and a choice instead of shouting back.
